data.title: Ping An eyes Hong Kong ETFs after nod on cross-border investmentChina’s largest insurer downplays tax changes, shares positive outlook after reporting 36 per cent profit growth.
data.description:
Ping An Insurance (Group), China’s largest insurer in terms of market capitalisation, is eyeing investments in Hong Kong-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to boost returns following Beijing’s green light for cross-border allocations, according to senior executives.
“Allowing mainland insurance funds to invest in Hong Kong listed ETFs is set to tighten the ties between Hong Kong and the mainland capital market,” said Richard Sheng, secretary of the company’s board, after a press conference on Friday. “We will consider various opportunities, including Hong Kong ETFs, in our insurance allocation strategy.”
The National Financial Regulatory Administration (NFRA) voiced support on Tuesday for insurance funds investing in ETFs through the Stock Connect schemes, which allow cross-border trading between the mainland China and Hong Kong financial markets.
The average daily turnover of ETFs – index funds that track certain stocks – in Hong Kong reached HK$40.6 billion (US$5.2 billion) in the first seven months of 2026, up 22 per cent from a year earlier, according to Hong Kong stock exchange data.
“Many Hong Kong ETFs offer exposure to non‑Hong Kong and non‑mainland assets, including overseas investments and various thematic strategies,” said Kenny Tang Sing-hing, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators. “This can enrich mainland insurers’ investment instruments and strategies, potentially boosting returns without them having to rely solely on Hong Kong or mainland markets.”
For Hong Kong’s ETF market, the benefit was “even more obvious”, he said, as insurance capital was typically long‑term and stable, helping to reduce market volatility.
Meanwhile, Ping An executives said they were not worried about Beijing’s recent tightening of control over cross-border investment.
“The tax policy is not new,” said Xie Yonglin, executive director, president and co-CEO of Ping An. “The tax policy doesn’t yet apply to domestic insurance income, and Ping An’s overseas policy-related business sector is small, so overall impact is negligible.”
[Hong Kong ETFs] can enrich mainland insurers’ investment instruments and strategies, potentially boosting returns
Kenny Tang, Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators
Beijing in recent months has stepped up controls on wealthy mainland families’ use of cross-border wealth management and insurance products. Some local authorities enforced a 20 per cent tax on gains from offshore insurance policies as part of that push earlier this month.
Such taxes would reduce the returns of policies bought in Hong Kong and thus enhance the competitiveness of mainland-issued insurance policies. Hong Kong insurance policies invest more in international stocks and bonds, and hence usually provide a higher return than mainland policies, which face more restrictions.
Xie said the outlook for the insurer was positive after it reported 36 per cent growth in first-half net profit on Thursday, driven by investment income and sales growth.
“The overall economic environment is remaining low-interest-rate for the long term, narrowing the spread for the financial industry, but the life insurance industry on the contrary is entering a golden era, because life insurance offers long-term guaranteed returns and stable yields even in such an environment,” he said.
Mainland insurance companies held total assets of 41.31 trillion yuan (US$6.1 trillion) at the end of last year, according to government statistics. As some of the largest institutional investors in the equity markets, they tend to make long-term commitments, typically spanning a decade or more.
Beijing has rolled out a number of measures since early 2025, including relaxing capital requirements, to allow mainland insurers to invest between 30 and 40 per cent of their assets in stocks, up from 10 to 20 per cent previously, depending on their asset size.

data.title: China’s telecoms giants bet on ‘token factories’ as AI drives revenue growth
data.description:
China’s three state-owned telecoms giants have made billable artificial intelligence tokens a key focus of their growth strategies, as AI adoption accelerates across the country and computing demand soars.
China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom all pointed to AI and computing operations as key growth drivers in their first-half financial disclosures released this month, presenting usage of tokens – the fundamental unit of data processed by AI models – as a central metric alongside others such as compute power and data.
On Thursday, China Telecom announced it had recorded a 95 per cent surge in intelligent computing revenue during the first half of the year. That drove a 7.1 per cent increase in its broader “intelligent business” revenue to 31.1 billion yuan (US$4.6 billion).
The carrier highlighted the token packages it now offered to mobile users nationwide, as well as a recent upgrade to its Xingchen TokenHub platform, which hosts 142 large language models and more than 420 industry-specific AI applications.
The company said it had also upgraded Xirang, its orchestration software for compute resources and networks, extending support to more than 20 chip architectures. Meanwhile, China Telecom Cloud revenue rose 7.8 per cent to 61.8 billion yuan.
China Unicom, which reported earnings on Tuesday, posted 41.9 billion yuan in computing-power revenue – a 13 per cent increase across data centres, leased compute, business software and cloud-based AI.
In its filing, Unicom pointed to its launch of a “token supermarket” – part of an end-to-end ecosystem to create, transfer, store and use AI tokens. Its UniAI platform connected more than 200 large language models and collected over 500 terabytes of high-quality data, it said.


Underscoring its aggressive expansion plans, Unicom’s capital expenditure on compute infrastructure surged by more than 80 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026, and accounted for more than one-third of the firm’s total capex.
China Mobile, which kicked off the telecoms reporting cycle on August 13, logged 52.9 billion yuan in computing-services revenue during the first six months, up 14 per cent, while AI-services revenue edged up 0.9 per cent to 49.3 billion yuan.
Computing and AI services combined accounted for 22.6 per cent of China Mobile’s principal business revenue over the period. High-performance computing revenue used to train and run models grew over 130 per cent to 5.3 billion yuan.
China Mobile outlined a “token factory” strategy combining models, compute and data-centre capacity, alongside regional token-product pilots and its MoMA platform, which gives enterprise users access to multiple AI models.
None of the three operators disclosed stand-alone token revenues, active customer counts, monthly consumption metrics or profit margins.
State carriers are not alone in monetising this shift towards a token economy.
Chinese AI solutions provider Phancy Group, formerly known as 4Paradigm, said revenue from its application programming interface services – which allow external enterprise applications to connect directly to the AI models it hosts – had surged over 860 per cent year on year to 460 million yuan, as token consumption rose about 620 per cent.
According to China’s National Data Administration, domestic average daily AI token calls surpassed 140 trillion in March, up from just 100 billion two years earlier. That is equivalent to roughly 100,000 tokens per person based on the country’s population of about 1.4 billion.

data.title: What’s next for Alibaba as US$56 billion AI spending plan hits halfway mark?Aggressive spending strains cash, but Alibaba’s AI cloud growth points to strong long-term returns, analysts say.
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding is expected to further accelerate cloud growth, expand operating margins and achieve faster payback on artificial intelligence investments, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant reaches the halfway mark of its massive 380 billion yuan (US$56 billion) AI infrastructure spending plan.
“The most important incremental message, in our view, is that cloud growth has not yet peaked,” Nomura analysts said in a research note on Friday.
The comment followed Alibaba’s Thursday report of a 45 per cent revenue increase in its cloud and AI businesses for the three months ended June, marking the fastest growth in 22 quarters.
“This accelerating growth is occurring alongside meaningful margin expansion rather than at the expense of profitability,” Nomura analysts wrote, highlighting that the AI cloud unit’s adjusted Ebita margin reached 11.6 per cent, up from about 7 per cent a year ago.
Jefferies expected revenue growth for Alibaba’s Cloud and Compute Services, the company’s new reporting segment covering its cloud business and T-Head chip arm, to accelerate beyond 50 per cent year on year in the September quarter, with momentum building further into the next two quarters through March 2027.
We believe Alibaba’s results have delivered positive developments around cloud growth as a bright spot
Goldman Sachs
For the first time, the company provided clear visibility to investors on payoffs from its AI capital expenditures (capex). During an earnings call on Thursday, group CEO Eddie Wu Yongming said its AI computing investments would break even within three years – or possibly two as gross margins rose.
Wu said the company had already spent 190 billion yuan in capex as of the end of June, part of its plan announced last year to commit 380 billion yuan to digital infrastructure over the next three years.
Following the call, Goldman Sachs analysts lifted the capex estimates for its financial years 2027 and 2028 to 210 billion yuan and 240 billion yuan, respectively, driven by strong AI demand and favourable return on invested capital (ROIC) that prompted elevated spending.
“We believe Alibaba’s results have delivered positive developments around cloud growth as a bright spot, higher certainty on ROIC despite capex uplift, and an inflection in earnings per share growth with improving quick commerce unit economics,” Goldman Sachs said.
Shares of Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post, fell 2.5 per cent to close at HK$123 in Hong Kong on Friday.
While its 67.7 billion yuan quarterly outlay eclipsed the 52.8 billion yuan spent by domestic peer Tencent Holdings, the figures underscore a divergence in scale compared with US hyperscalers.
Major American tech giants – Amazon.com, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta Platforms – are collectively projected to spend around US$700 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, averaging US$44 billion per quarter per company.
One of Alibaba’s biggest financial concerns remains the increasing cash outflow under its aggressive spending plan. Free cash outflow in the June quarter more than doubled to 44.7 billion yuan year on year, as heavier investment in cloud infrastructure strained cash generation.
Analysts forecast that surging demand for compute and the deployment of proprietary AI chips would offset short-term cash flow pressures.
Wu also justified the spike in quarterly capex, citing procurement timing, additional central processing unit capacity to meet AI agent demand, and higher chip prices.
Wu offered a telling example of strong demand: Nvidia’s A100 cards purchased in 2020 and V100 cards purchased in 2018 were still running at full capacity in its data centres.
A central pillar of this return profile is Alibaba’s proprietary chipmaking arm, T-Head. Having shipped more than 500,000 units of its previous-generation chips cumulatively, Alibaba began commercialising T-Head’s latest Zhenwu M890 chips on its cloud in supernode form – designed to knit hundreds or thousands of chips together to act as one giant supercomputer – earlier this month.
Looking ahead, Wu said long-term revenue growth and margin expansion trends would be “exceptionally strong”, and as a result, the cloud unit was “highly confident” in its ability to achieve the goal of US$100 billion in external revenue by 2030.

data.title: Hong Kong and Shenzhen test crossings at revamped Huanggang Port ahead of opening
data.description:
Hong Kong has conducted its first test involving Shenzhen authorities of clearance procedures and private car access at the revamped Huanggang border crossing, ahead of a massive exercise next week involving 20,000 people to fully assess the facility’s capacity.
No 2 official Eric Chan Kwok-ki said Saturday’s drill went smoothly and passenger flows were orderly, with speedy pickup by public transport, although a motorist association reported traffic jams along the San Tin Interchange roundabout leading to the crossing.
“We will conduct a further stress test with a continuous peak-level passenger and traffic flow to ensure smooth operations,” Chan said, describing next Saturday’s exercise as a “large-scale cross-border drill”.
Hong Kong authorities have conducted several drills at the Huanggang Port crossing at the mainland Chinese border this month as a part of final preparations before the checkpoint opens, which sources have said could come as early as next month.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said next Saturday’s drill would increase pressure on capacity and feature a full test of 90 clearance channels within the building, as well as assess how private vehicles would use a new clearance machine.
“Through today’s exercise, we have identified further improvement measures, such as how to line up buses and different transport,” Tang added.
The latest 10,000-strong drill focused on vehicle clearance operations. Private cars were arranged to simulate the vehicle clearance process for entry to Shenzhen.
Cars first passed through a customs kiosk before immigration clearance to avoid having to back up midway through the clearance channel for a spot check.

Vehicles then stopped in front of the immigration checkpoint, where an “integrated information collective device” will complete the clearance, occupant temperature check and biometric data collection in one go, although the cars did not use the machine.
Authorities also tested how cars would turn back should problems with occupant identity documents arise or if they were refused entry by Shenzhen authorities.
Following the vehicle flow trial, dozens of civil servants used the “joint clearance” e-channels, equipped with three gates instead of the two in traditional clearance machines, to cross into Shenzhen.
The revamped checkpoint will be the first to deploy the “joint clearance” model, where people only need to show one type of identity document required by their destination for e-channel clearance.
Traditionally, crossing the border requires visiting a departure and arrival counter.
Authorities have staged three peak traffic stress tests, each involving about 2,000 civil servants crossing into Hong Kong and descending into the arrival hall.

Authorities also simulated situations where a passenger found to have a fever was sent for a further check and another in which a traveller was caught smuggling illicit cigarettes and an endangered tortoise into the city.
Ringo Lee Yiu-pui, honorary life president of the Hong Kong, China Automobile Association, told the South China Morning Post that 400 drivers had volunteered to take part in Saturday’s drill, with each car making at least two trips to the crossing.
Lee said the drivers had started out in Fanling and Sheung Shui, with the latter route along the Yuen Long Highway proving more congested.
Some drivers had taken a wrong turn at the San Tin Interchange roundabout, while others were slowed by works on roads leading to the port building and slip roads condensing into single-lane traffic.

A minor traffic accident also occurred at around 1pm at the interchange, he said, adding authorities could introduce clearer signage.
“In our experience, the time stuck in traffic could be as long as an hour, as besides the roundabout being jammed, roads leading to Huanggang would also be congested,” Lee said.
Tang said traffic flow leading to the crossing was “heavy but smooth”.

data.title: Hong Kong-built greenhouse gas tracker device ‘functioning well’ on space station
data.description:
A greenhouse gas monitoring instrument developed by a university in Hong Kong is operating successfully aboard the Tiangong space station and is expected to contribute to sustainable development, the city’s technology minister has said.
Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong also revealed more details in a blog post on Saturday about the life of the city’s first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, who he said had a busy schedule at the space station.
The Multi‑Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory (Musico), developed by a team led by scientists at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and funded by the city government, has been deployed to China’s space station.
“Musico is equipped with four sensors for detecting carbon dioxide, methane, oxygen, and aerosols. They have all successfully captured images with clear imaging quality and demonstrated good overall performance,” he said.
“Over the next two years or more, the instrument will provide autonomous, controllable, and highly accurate greenhouse gas (carbon dioxide and methane) emission monitoring data, contributing to efforts to address climate change and promote global sustainable development.”
Musico is considered the world’s first lightweight, high-resolution, high-precision synergistic observatory for carbon dioxide and methane.
Although the instrument is smaller than a household washing machine, it can accurately detect specific sources of greenhouse gas emissions on Earth, according to the university.

Five other projects, led by scholars from Polytechnic University, the University of Hong Kong, City University and the Chinese University of Hong Kong, had received funding from the special call for aerospace technology under the government’s Innovation and Technology Support Programme, Sun said.
The minister also revealed that Lai, who has been working at the space station for about three months, had “completed a series of experiments and scientific studies with her teammates, while also performing daily station maintenance, health monitoring and emergency pressure drills” amid a busy schedule.
He added that the government had brought nearly 400 local students to visit mainland China’s aerospace research bases during the summer holiday, with the aim of cultivating their interest in the area.
“I hope more and more Hong Kong youth will follow the example of Dr Lai, aim high, work hard and pursue their dreams in innovation and technology,” he said.

data.title: Man, 38, arrested for driving under the influence of drugs after 3-vehicle crash
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested a 38-year-old man for driving under the influence of drugs following a three-vehicle crash that led to two people being hospitalised.
Police said they received a report at 1.48pm on Saturday of a traffic accident along Pok Fu Lam Road involving a large truck and two light goods vehicles.
The force said the 38-year-old driver of one of the light goods vehicles failed a drug test that was administered at the scene.
He was arrested for driving under the influence of drugs and dangerous driving causing grievous bodily harm.
The 61-year-old male driver of the other light goods vehicle and a 59-year-old female passenger were injured during the accident and were sent to Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam for treatment.
The force added that the 56-year-old male driver of the large truck also complained of chest pain following the incident, but refused medical treatment.
The arrested driver has been detained pending further investigation.

data.title: Man hospitalised after bamboo scaffolding collapses in Sham Shui Po
data.description:
A Hong Kong man has been hospitalised after being trapped under a collapsed bamboo scaffolding at a building in Sham Shui Po.
Emergency services were called to 105-107 Nam Cheong Street at around 3.49pm on Saturday following reports of the incident.
A section of scaffolding secured to the building’s exterior wall, measuring around 15 metres (49 feet) by 33 metres, had partially collapsed, trapping the victim, who is believed to be in his fifties or sixties.
According to the force, the victim suffered head injuries but remained conscious throughout the rescue and was taken to Princess Margaret Hospital in Kwai Chung for treatment.
Police have classified the case as an industrial accident, and an investigation into the cause of the collapse is ongoing.

data.title: Hong Kong police arrest 2 men allegedly linked to HK$500,000 phishing scam
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested two men suspected of using 110 SIM cards in a hotel room to send phishing messages, conning victims of more than HK$500,000 (US$63,766).
The force said on Saturday that the men, aged 31 and 44, were arrested last Thursday on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud.
They were allegedly linked to recent phishing scams in which fraudsters posed as delivery company staff, claiming victims had undelivered parcels, or as employees of online payment platforms, saying victims had to pay a fee to cancel an insurance plan they had mistakenly subscribed to. Victims were then induced to call a fake customer service hotline.
After victims called the hotline, the fraudsters instructed them to transfer money to designated bank accounts using various pretexts, police said.
“Investigation revealed that the suspects had bought a bulk of SIM cards with real name registration from different people,” inspector Kwan Yat-hei of the fraud division under the force’s commercial crime bureau said.
He added that the suspects had rented a hotel room as an operations centre. Officers found a modem pool – a device that allows users to control multiple SIM cards simultaneously – as well as nine mobile phones and 110 SIM cards in the room.
Investigators found that the suspects had sent more than 2,000 suspected scam messages.
“We found some of the intercepted phone numbers were related to some recently reported scam cases, involving more than HK$500,000,” Kwan said.
He added that the pair remained in custody pending further investigation and that more arrests were possible.
Kwan urged residents not to call numbers shown in suspicious messages. They should also not lend or sell their SIM cards to others.
“If any SIM cards were used for fraud or other illicit activities, people lending or selling the cards were assisting with crimes and may be subject to criminal liability,” he said.
Under Hong Kong law, conspiracy to defraud carries a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment.
Since March 2022, all SIM cards in Hong Kong have been required to undergo real-name registration using users’ identification documents.

data.title: Customs seizes endangered turtles and parrots in 2 cases, arrests woman
data.description:
Hong Kong customs officers have seized endangered turtles and parrots alongside other animals in two separate smuggling cases, resulting in the arrest of one woman.
The Customs and Excise Department said on Saturday that 17 live turtles were discovered in a package declared as containing a jacket arriving at Hong Kong International Airport from the United States.
“Upon inspection, a batch of live turtles of suspected scheduled endangered species was found concealed in socks,” it said.
Customs estimated the market value of the turtles at about HK$102,000 (US$13,010).
In a separate case on Friday, customs officers stopped a 21-year-old mainland Chinese woman arriving at the Lok Ma Chau Spur Line control point.
A search revealed a rabbit, hamster, guinea pig, sugar glider and two parrots suspected to be endangered species in a paper bag she was carrying and in a pocket of her trousers.
The animals had an estimated market value of about HK$7,800, and the woman was arrested.

Both cases have been handed over to the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department for follow-up investigation.
In Hong Kong, the unlawful import, export or possession of endangered animals can result in a fine of up to HK$10 million and 10 years in jail.
Additionally, anyone found guilty of illegally importing animals, carcasses or animal products is liable to a maximum fine of HK$50,000 and imprisonment for one year. It is also an offence to import any bird unless it is accompanied by a valid health certificate.

data.title: Government still weighing decision on restricting proxy voters, official says
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities have yet to decide whether to restrict proxy voters at homeowners’ meetings to relatives or other flat owners of the same estate under proposed law amendments meant to combat bid-rigging, the home affairs director has said, arguing such a move could be overly strict.
Director of Home Affairs Priscilla To Kit-lai said on Saturday that the proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance were aimed at enhancing the legitimacy of proxy votes amid concerns that voting results could be manipulated by a minority.
But she said the government had yet to decide whether proxy holders should be limited to the owners’ relatives or other owners in the same estate.
“For example, an elderly person living alone has a familiar friend in a different housing estate who helps the person – that’s acceptable now,” she said on a television programme.
“But it might not be possible if we add proposed restrictions. We need to see if society feels this is too strict.”
Issues of building management and owner governance came under intense scrutiny during an independent committee hearing looking into the cause of the devastating fire at Wang Fuk Court that killed 168 people last November, with testimonies alleging bid-rigging and proxy vote collection.
In a consultation document released earlier this month, authorities laid out five major directions for proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance, which regulates incorporated ownership in buildings.
The five suggestions comprised imposing a higher attendance requirement and voting thresholds for decisions on large-scale and high-value maintenance procurement, improving the proxy vote system; optimising the process for declaration of interests; strengthening authorities’ powers; and clarifying meeting procedures.

To said electronic voting was not included due to identity verification issues.
“Currently, a Hong Kong identity card is required for the ‘iAM Smart’ app account, but a significant number of property owners in Hong Kong may be overseas residents without a Hong Kong identity card,” she said. “We need to resolve these technical issues.”
The app is the government’s digital authentication platform.
Asked whether the government could directly step in to remove a management committee if its chairman refused to convene a meeting without reasonable justification, To said authorities needed to consider individual rights.
“Building management is the responsibility of the homeowners, and ownership is their private property. Therefore, when considering when to intervene, another aspect we need to balance is the power of the public,” she said.
“It’s crucial to balance the importance of individual rights, so the government will not rashly intervene at this time.”

data.title: Hong Kong hits back at Western ‘slander’ over verdict on Tiananmen vigil leaders
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities have hit out at what they called “baseless slander and smearing” by Western countries over the conviction of the now-disbanded alliance behind the annual Tiananmen Square vigil and its leaders for inciting subversion, stressing the court’s verdict is “well-reasoned and sound”.
The government issued a strongly worded statement on Saturday after the closely-watched verdict on the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China a day earlier sparked a chorus of criticism from several Western countries and the United Nations over suppression of freedom.
Three High Court judges ruled that any attempt to overthrow or undermine the Communist Party of China’s leadership could constitute a subversion offence because the country’s constitution did not permit Western-style democracy.
They found the Hong Kong Alliance, its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung had incited public hatred towards the party by likening Beijing’s crackdown on protesters in 1989 to local authorities’ suppression of the 2019 anti-government demonstrations. The fourth defendant Albert Ho Chun-yan had earlier pleaded guilty.
A government spokesman said on Saturday it strongly condemned the “baseless slander and smearing” against the city by “various Western countries, anti-China media, organisations and politicians” over the case.
He defended the ruling of the court, citing the judges had also pointed out that the defendants had all along been hostile towards the Communist Party and the central government under its leadership.
“The reasons for verdict handed down by the court clearly emphasised that the defendants were put on trial not because of their political views or beliefs,” he said.
“The court would only consider the laws and evidence relevant to the case to decide whether the prosecution is able to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt.”
The spokesman also said the defendants had refused to “pull back from the brink” after the imposition of the national security law in 2020 and were “bent on embracing the resistance line of the alliance to the very end”.
“The defendants intended to cause others to lose confidence in the [Communist Party] by stirring up hostility and causing division, so as to achieve the objective of undermining the fundamental system of the People’s Republic of China. Their conspiracy was abundantly clear, which must be brought to justice,” he said.

Authorities said the convicted defendants’ rights to a fair trial had been safeguarded by the Basic Law and the Hong Kong Bill of Rights, and the judiciary had exercised its power independently.
“The verdict handed down by the court in this case is forceful and compelling, as well as well-reasoned and sound, meticulously explained the court’s analysis of the relevant legal principles and evidence, as well as the reasons for the conviction,” it said.
“Members of the public should not be misled by the external forces’ attempts to smear, but must be able to distinguish between right and wrong, and clearly understand the difference between this case and the normal situation regarding the exercise of freedoms of association, assembly and speech.”
Set up after the 1989 Tiananmen Square movement, the alliance had long organised vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to honour the event, and called for “ending one-party dictatorship” in China.
A three-judge panel on Friday said that while it was not unlawful for the alliance to organise vigils to mark the crackdown, the defendants had used the annual event to attract new supporters and instigate them to take action to oust the ruling party.
The verdict had drawn criticism from many Western governments, including the United Kingdom, European Union, France, Germany, Australia and the United States, who slammed the conviction as suppression of freedom.
United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres also chipped in on Friday through his spokesman, arguing people should be allowed to speak without fear of arrest and prosecution.
Inciting subversion in Hong Kong carries a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment under the national security law. Any company or organisation that commits an offence under the law can be handed a fine of an indefinite sum.
The panel of judges will hear oral mitigation arguments on August 28 before delivering the sentences.

data.title: Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says
data.description:
About 280,000 patients have secured full fee waivers since Hong Kong’s public healthcare fee reform took effect at the start of the year — a 20-fold increase from the previous figure of 14,000, the health minister has said.
Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau revealed the figures on Saturday as he defended the reform, which raised user fees for non-urgent and less serious services to reduce the government subsidy rate. He said the changes were intended to optimise the use of existing resources and strengthen protection for vulnerable groups.
“Since its implementation, just in eight months the number of people benefiting from full medical fee waivers has increased from 14,000 to 280,000—a growth of over 20-fold,” he said.
The new public healthcare fee regime was introduced on January 1 to ensure the sustainable development of the healthcare system amid challenges posed by an ageing population.
Under the new fee structure, a visit to an accident and emergency department at a public hospital costs HK$400 (US$51) for less urgent cases, up from between HK$50 and HK$150 per visit.

The number of people eligible for subsidised or free healthcare will also expand significantly, from 300,000 to 1.4 million, following the relaxation of income and asset limits.
Lo said the government previously subsidised up to 97.6 per cent of public healthcare costs, representing a significant public benefit.
“Following the healthcare reform, our goal is to shift towards a user-pays model under which those who can afford should pay. Currently, government subsidies still stand at 95 per cent. We aim to gradually reduce them to 90 per cent within five years,” he said.
“Please be assured that those facing financial hardship will remain fully exempt from fees.”
Lo added that the Hospital Authority was also reviewing whether innovative drugs and medical devices could be introduced more quickly, with the aim of speeding up public access through the mechanism without placing a heavy financial burden on patients.
He said the approval process for subsidised drugs had accelerated since the fee reform, with 17 medications — including specialist drugs — added to the drug registry so far this year.
“For example, there was a targeted therapy drug used to treat blood cancer. Before the fee reform and the speeding up of the relevant approval mechanisms, patients had to pay out of pocket between HK$20,000 and HK$40,000,” he said. “Now, patients pay only HK$20 every four weeks if the drug is prescribed.”

data.title: Beyblade battles drive up sales at Hong Kong malls, but will the trend last?
data.description:
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “Three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.
Dish-shaped plastic battle arenas known as “Beystadiums” have been set up not only in Tuen Mun Town Plaza, but also across the mall in different shops, where some players challenge shop staff to collect stamps for shopping vouchers.
The spinning toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and across Asia early this year, with local fans flocking to public arenas to battle against other players and scrambling to buy hot models and rare parts.
Spotting the economic potential behind the hobby, local shopping centre operators across Hong Kong are converting public spaces into free battle zones to drive up foot traffic and sales and retain visitors.
The Tuen Mun Town Plaza even went a step further by scaling up the concept into a mall-wide strategy ahead of a major Beyblade tournament in August, encouraging shop operators to take part in the game and offer discounts to shoppers who present their tops.
“The strategy is about how a tenant can engage with customers through a shared interest, instead of directly selling to them,” said Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer of Sino Group, which owns the shopping centre.
“It’s a soft-selling approach that allows staff and shoppers to start a conversation, drawing people into the store before making a sales pitch.”

What appeared to be a desperate measure by Hong Kong’s retail and catering sectors – still struggling with the trend of residents heading to mainland China for cheaper shopping and dining options – turned into an initial success.
Chhoa said the shopping centre had witnessed a “noticeable” 20 per cent surge in holiday foot traffic at the shopping centre after the promotion, as well as a 10 to 15 per cent rise in weekday attendance.
All in the game
At Hanamaruken, a ramen shop inside the Tuen Mun complex, co-founder Jelly Tong said her team upgraded the basic Beyblade provided by the landlord to a high-performance model to better compete with visiting players as they recognised the game’s potential to drive up business.
“Words then spread in their Beyblade chat groups that our store had an exceptionally strong setup, and some kids ended up bringing six or seven friends over to challenge us,” Tong said. “Afterwards, they stayed here to eat and discuss our custom gear.”
The commercial benefits have extended beyond restaurants and toy retailers to high-end luxury tenants like Luk Fook Jewellery. A regional manager said that setting up an in-store battle station helped break down traditional stereotypes surrounding luxury retail.
“We saw many new faces coming in after matching with our staff to browse our products and some actually made transactions,” said Patrick Ng Pui-kuen, the brand’s New Territories West district manager, who oversees the branches in Tuen Mun.
Among dozens of enthusiasts gathered at the shopping complex were 24-year-old warehouse worker Liu Chun-yin and his friend.
“Sometimes I show my spinning top at the nearby ice cream shop here to get special offers, or battle against the staff at the tea shop to win a discount,” Liu said.
His friend, a recent Beyblade fan, recalled a visit where he stayed at the venue from 2pm until 9pm, spending seven hours straight battling fellow players and purchasing food and drinks in between matches.

Over in D-Park in Tsuen Wan, dedicated free-play zones equipped with rows of desks have also drawn parents with young children alongside seasoned adult hobbyists.
Andy Yip, a 34-year-old civil servant from Kowloon East, made a dedicated trip to Tsuen Wan with his 11-year-old son and other family members, knowing there would be players at the venue.
“Before my son picked up the hobby, we spent most of our weekends in mainland China, but now we stay more in Hong Kong to accompany him, as he wants to play Beyblade with others,” he said.
Yip added that these outings were typically paired with dining and retail shopping, noting that he typically spent HK$1,000 (US$128) on dinner after his son played at D-Park, while their family members browsed at nearby shops during matches.
At Pioneer Centre in Prince Edward, a similar trend has recently unfolded, with management introducing a few Beyblade stadiums to attract a steady stream of parents and children, and launching a spend-to-draw promotion that offered exclusive models of the tops as prizes.
Eric Cheng, senior leasing manager at the mall, said the setup and promotion in August had driven a 5 to 10 per cent increase in foot traffic compared with the same period last year, while sales at electronic goods and food and beverage outlets had jumped by 15 and 20 per cent, respectively.
“Compared with other intellectual property (IP) photo spots or traditional pop-ups, Beyblade’s interactive nature brings us much higher foot traffic,” Cheng said.
“Visitors at photo spots often leave after taking pictures, while playing Beyblade at the mall gets them to stay longer.”
Cheng said that longer stays could translate to higher spending as shoppers sought food and beverage options in between battles.
Only a short-term cure?
For all its resurgent popularity, the Beyblade trend offered only short-term benefits and was a temporary solution rather than a cure-all for the city’s broader retail sector challenges, according to one economist.
Professor Terence Chong Tai-leung, executive director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance, said shopping centres were ideal venues for Beyblade matches, which required space, and operators could set up play zones at a low cost.
“On a micro level, it drives temporary F&B spending as visitors have a reason to come,” Chong said, noting that overall retail has still failed to show significant growth over the past year.

But he stressed that such initiatives were insufficient to counter broader macroeconomic headwinds or the trend of residents spending across the border, pointing out that price remained the most significant factor driving consumer behaviour.
To stay relevant in the long run, Chong suggested that local malls rethink their structural function, shifting from traditional sales hubs towards specialised themed venues or physical showrooms.
“Most successful malls in Hong Kong have distinct themes, and if you want to attract people, you have to concentrate,” he said. “For example, becoming the definitive hub for sneakers so that people will visit whenever they want to buy sneakers.”
Chong also suggested malls evolve into showrooms where customers preview products before purchasing them online, rather than relying solely on traditional storefront sales.
“Due to structural shifts in shopping habits, consumer needs that used to require a mall visit can now be easily met through various online platforms.”

data.title: OpenAI-backed legal tech firm pivots to Chinese Kimi K3 open-weight model
data.description:
A US artificial intelligence start-up backed by OpenAI has built its first in-house model on Chinese lab Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, highlighting a growing shift by Western tech firms towards Chinese open-weight systems amid soaring development costs.
San Francisco-based legal tech provider Harvey, whose high-profile backers also include Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, said on Thursday that its new model, Harvey Tenet, was post-trained on top of the open-weight Kimi K3 base.
The company said the system achieved “state-of-the-art” performance in complex legal work.
The release marks a significant departure for Harvey, which serves major international law firms and enterprise clients. The start-up previously focused on customising closed proprietary models from US leaders such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for legal applications.
Harvey’s pivot was “a great example of open-weight models” enabling developers to post-train systems on specific industry or corporate data for higher accuracy and lower inference costs, AI policy researcher Simon Hedlin wrote on social media on Friday.
Post-training is the process of refining a general-purpose base model with specialised data sets to excel at specific tasks.

“We’re still only in the very earliest stages of exploring what’s possible to do with highly capable open-weight models,” Hedlin said.
“It’s unfortunate that America is lagging behind in developing frontier open-weight models.”
Founded in the summer of 2022, the start-up reached a valuation of US$11 billion in a financing round in March.
Harvey said in a blog post on Thursday that its research over the past six months focused on building “frontier legal intelligence using open-weight models” and enabling law firms to build and deploy specialised models.
Trained on comprehensive legal data sets, Harvey Tenet outperformed both its underlying base model and US frontier systems – including Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol – across a range of complex, long-horizon legal agentic tasks, according to the company.
The approach also improved cost efficiency, according to Harvey. The firm said that while open-weight models naturally offered lower per token prices, it also worked on reducing the number of tokens consumed in inference.
The training for Harvey Tenet was done over two months using around 150 Nvidia B300 graphics processing units (GPUs), the company said.
Open-source models such as Nvidia’s Nemotron series now account for 40 per cent of US telecommunications giant AT&T’s employee AI queries, according to a Thursday report by The Information, citing AT&T vice-president Mark Austin.
Austin reportedly also said that AT&T was not currently using any Chinese open-weight models.
The company was still “evaluating the potential risks” of using them, he reportedly said, and analysing options from Chinese firms including DeepSeek and Moonshot, the Beijing-based company behind Kimi K3.

data.title: Parts shortage piles pressure on Chinese carmakers racing to boost intelligence
data.description:
Chinese smart vehicle makers have been hit by another setback as a global components shortage collides with surging prices of raw materials, driven by the artificial intelligence boom.
It would take at least a year for the global supply chain to ramp up production of printed circuit boards (PCBs) and multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) – two key parts that make vehicles intelligent – to meet rising demand, according to industry officials and analysts.
“The components, though small, play a key role in the automotive industry’s effort to make millions of cars more autonomous and smarter,” Chen Jinzhu, CEO of the consultancy Shanghai Mingliang Auto Service, told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday.
“Market demand for electric vehicles [EVs] is falling, but component supply remains a thorny issue for leading players since they focus on intelligence to make their cars attractive to consumers.”
Industry officials said the global auto sector was facing a 20 to 30 per cent shortage of components, with prices more than tripling over the past year.
Carmakers’ cost pressure mainly comes from memory chips. But a lack of PCBs and MLCCs disrupts production and prevents assemblies from running smoothly
Dai Yong, Geely Auto
The crunch stems from explosive AI growth and the rapid buildout of AI data centres worldwide.
PCBs are widely used along with graphics processing units and application-specific integrated circuits to support AI applications. They are also needed to make mobile phones, digital devices and cars.
Data from the India Printed Circuit Association showed that PCB prices had surged more than threefold over the past 12 months to about 330 yuan (US$49) per sheet.
MLCCs, dubbed the “rice of the electronics industry”, are tiny electronic components that regulate and stabilise electrical currents in devices ranging from smartphones and EVs to AI servers and data centres.
Prices of some MLCC components increased from 10 yuan per 1,000 units to 40 yuan in early 2026 amid a severe shortage caused by surging demand from AI servers and data centres, according to traders.
Dai Yong, chief financial officer of Geely Auto, mainland China’s second-largest carmaker, said in an interview on Monday that the price jumps in the two components had a minimal impact on earnings because the parts remained a small slice of the total expenses.
“Carmakers’ cost pressure mainly comes from memory chips,” he said. “But a lack of PCBs and MLCCs disrupts production and prevents assemblies from running smoothly.”
Dai added that memory chips for data buffering, processing and storage – essential to autonomous driving – had been squeezing carmakers’ profit margins since early 2026.
Market know-how can effectively help us plan ahead
Lily Cai, Ecarx
Carmakers and automotive supply chain vendors were forced to scramble for chips at lofty prices as the rapid rise of AI generated massive orders.
Memory chips used in the AI industry were more sophisticated and expensive, generating higher added value for manufacturers, who would typically allocate more products to hi-tech clients, rather than EV makers and car component producers, Qian Kang, an owner of a vehicle circuit board factory in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, told the SCMP on Wednesday.
To secure enough parts, carmakers are paying steep premiums for everything from memory chips to MLCCs to keep production running.
William Li, CEO of Shanghai-based premium EV maker Nio, said last month that surging raw material prices, particularly memory chips, had added 20,000 yuan to the production cost of each vehicle. He admitted that carmakers were under heavy pressure to stay afloat.
Ecarx, a tech firm that provides hardware and software known as the “intelligent brain” for digital cockpits and preliminary self-driving systems, said strong innovative capability and a full-stack development platform could help companies dodge risks in an undersupplied market.
Lily Cai, executive vice-president of Ecarx, said car parts suppliers with deep market knowledge could anticipate trends by working closely with upstream manufacturers to develop new products and technologies.
“Market know-how can effectively help us plan ahead,” she said. “Ecarx established multiple major partnerships with key component suppliers to deepen innovation as early as last year. Those collaborative efforts gave us an advantage in securing sufficient supply and outpacing our peers in product development.”
In the second half of 2025, Ecarx signed agreements with PCB maker Victory Giant Technology, semiconductor firm Monolithic Power Systems and tech giant Samsung to build high-performance, AI-powered computing platforms for intelligent vehicles.
Analysts warned that despite the mainland market’s falling sales, a push by manufacturers to build smarter cars could worsen shortages.
Overall deliveries on the mainland, including petrol-powered cars and EVs, plunged 21 per cent year on year in July to 1.46 million units, according to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA).
Some 12 per cent of new cars priced between 150,000 yuan and 200,000 yuan were fitted with lidar sensors, which help cars map terrain, in 2025. The proportion climbed to 27 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, CPCA data showed.

data.title: Labour unions call for mandatory heatstroke-prevention equipment for workers
data.description:
Hong Kong labour unionists have called for employers to be required to provide outdoor workers with heatstroke-prevention equipment during extreme temperatures.
They also said on Saturday that heatstroke should be added to the list of statutory occupational diseases, making it easier for workers to claim compensation in work-related cases.
The calls for better protection for workers in extreme heat came after the city recorded unprecedented temperatures earlier this month.
Chau Sze-kit, chairman of the Hong Kong Construction Industry Employees General Union, said many workers urgently needed fan-cooled jackets, which could cost more than HK$1,000 (US$128) each and placed an additional financial burden on them.
He called for employers to be required to provide fan-cooled jackets, as they do safety helmets.
“Workers told us that fan-cooled jackets were the most effective personal protective equipment because wearing one could help lower the body temperature,” he told a radio programme.
“Our laws and regulations should keep pace with the times. Safety helmets weren’t required before but were added later.
“As fan-cooled jackets have now become a necessity, we should take this opportunity during our discussions to consider requiring employers by law to provide them to our workers during hot weather.”
Lawmaker Lam Chun-sing, chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions, suggested that tender documents should clearly set out requirements for personal heatstroke-prevention equipment, as well as compensation arrangements for project delays caused by heatwaves.
“We hope additional resources can be allocated to help us deal with adverse weather,” he said.
“For example, could equipment requirements be clearly specified in tender documents? Furthermore, if adverse weather, such as extreme heat, causes project delays, could compensation be available if certain criteria are met?”

Lam also called for heatstroke to be added to the list of statutory occupational diseases, saying workers currently found it difficult to prove that their cases were directly related to their jobs.
“If the disease is added as a statutory occupational disease, then workers do not need to prove that much. They just need to meet criteria such as time, work process and the type of work, and will get compensation,” he said.
He added that thresholds or requirements for heatstroke could be established, as with other statutory occupational diseases.
“If certain types of work involve a particularly high amount of outdoor conditions, or if their outdoor work time exceeds a certain number of hours, there is actually a direct relationship between the work and heatstroke,” he said.
Former Hong Kong Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying also said objective indicators would benefit workers.
“Set an objective indicator first. If a certain time limit or threshold is passed, it is presumed to be heatstroke. The burden of proof then shifts to the employer to prove that it isn’t. This makes the matter much easier for workers,” he said.
He also suggested that Hong Kong adopt the mechanism used in mainland China, where daily maximum temperatures of 35, 37 and 40 degrees Celsius trigger different heat-prevention measures.
The Labour Department recently drew criticism after its Heat Stress at Work Warning system remained at the lowest level despite the Observatory recording a peak temperature of 36.9 degrees Celsius (103 Fahrenheit) at its Tsim Sha Tsui headquarters on August 9 – the highest there since records began in 1884.
Employers are encouraged to give workers additional rest breaks under an amber warning, suspend very heavy labour under a red warning and halt heavy work under a black warning.
Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said earlier that authorities aimed to complete the revamp of the warning system by the end of this month.

data.title: Tesla forced to recall record 3 million cars in China over door-handle issue
data.description:
Tesla has issued the largest-ever product recall in mainland China’s electric vehicle (EV) market, as Elon Musk’s firm pledges to fix a door-handle issue affecting nearly 3 million cars.
The massive recall comes as Chinese regulators move to ban retractable car door handles over safety fears, after a fatal incident last year in which a driver was left trapped inside a burning vehicle as passers-by were unable to open the car doors.
While Tesla is not the only company affected by the move, the US firm has issued the largest recall announced so far.
The company will call back a total of 2.98 million vehicles, including Shanghai-made Model 3s and Model Ys as well as other cars imported from the United States, according to a statement issued by China’s State Administration for Market Regulation on Friday.
From September 25, Tesla will add warning labels to its cars’ internal door handles after the vehicles are recalled. The US carmaker will also conduct an over-the-air (OTA) update to its window-control software, which will lower a car’s windows after a collision.
“The door problem has become a big issue since late last year as Chinese regulators and passengers attached greater importance to safety,” said Zhang Wenjie, who runs a car maintenance workshop in Shanghai.
“It is expected by the market that large-scale recalls by Tesla and other domestic carmakers will eventually raise the auto industry’s awareness of product design and quality.”
Also on Friday, Xiaomi, a key rival to Tesla on the mainland, announced plans to recall about 400,000 vehicles over the car door issue.


Public concerns over the safety of car doors first erupted in October, after a fatal accident in southwest China’s Sichuan province involving a Xiaomi SU7 Ultra electric car.
According to local media reports, passers-by tried to pull a 31-year-old man out of the burning car, but could not open the doors.
In February, China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology announced its plan to ban retractable car door handles.
From next year, cars must have both internal and external door handles that can be mechanically opened at all times, even in the event of an accident or power failure, according to the new rules.
Separately, Tesla is also recalling 2.74 million Model 3 and Model Y vehicles assembled at its Shanghai factory to conduct another OTA software update to ensure its assisted steering and other driver-assistance functions are engaged when drivers fail to respond quickly during collisions, according to the regulator’s statement.
Tesla’s Shanghai Gigafactory began building Model 3 vehicles at the end of 2019, and it is now the US carmaker’s largest production base worldwide.
In 2025, the plant churned out about 851,000 vehicles for sale both in China and overseas. That represented more than half of Tesla’s total output that year, which dropped 8.6 per cent to 1.63 million units.
China is Tesla’s second-largest market worldwide, behind only the US.

data.title: Hong Kong to assess typhoon warning as Tropical Storm Narra nears Guangdong coast
data.description:
Hong Kong’s weather forecaster will assess next week whether to issue a typhoon warning as Tropical Storm Narra is expected to edge closer to the western Guangdong coast.
The Hong Kong Observatory said on Saturday morning that the storm was expected to linger over the vicinity of Beibu Wan, also known as the Gulf of Tonkin, before having a higher chance to turn east to northeast gradually early next week.
“The Observatory will closely monitor its movement and the change in local wind conditions, and assess the need for issuing tropical cyclone warning signals early next week,” it said.
The projected movement of Narra – named after a species of tree in the Philippines – would see the cyclone edging closer to the vicinity of Leizhou Peninsula and the coast of western Guangdong.
The forecaster said the week ahead would be cloudy and rainy, with coastal areas becoming windier and experiencing occasional heavy showers and squally thunderstorms from early to midweek. Sunny intervals are not expected to return until Friday.

As of 8am on Saturday, Narra was about 650km (403 miles) west of Hong Kong, packing maximum sustained winds of 65km/h (40mph) near its centre.
The tropical storm is expected to strengthen over the next few days. The observatory has estimated Narra’s maximum sustained wind speed to increase to 85km/h on Sunday and Monday.
Narra is expected to weaken into a tropical depression on Wednesday, with maximum wind speed expected to decrease to 55km/h.
The No 1 Standby Signal may be issued when a tropical cyclone is centred within about 800km of Hong Kong and may affect the city.

data.title: Hong Kong physiotherapists face job crunch amid oversupply and budget cuts
data.description:
Hong Kong physiotherapy graduates are facing a job crunch amid ongoing healthcare budget cuts and a surge in new practitioners entering the industry, with one representative saying 60 applicants had competed for one position in a remote care facility for elderly residents.
Data also showed that the proportion of applicants admitted to Polytechnic University’s (PolyU) prestigious physiotherapy programme who ranked it among their top three choices – known as “Band A” – fell by around 9 percentage points from last year, suggesting the institution was selecting more students who were less committed to the profession.
In an interview with the South China Morning Post earlier this month, Alexander Woo Chuen-hau, president of the Hong Kong Physiotherapy Association, said that job competition in the industry had intensified since 2025.
“There is an underlying demand for physiotherapists, but there is simply no budget to hire them after healthcare cuts became more pronounced in 2026, forcing all organisations to tighten their belts,” Woo said.
He was referring to the government’s announcement last year of recurrent public expenditure cuts of 1 to 2 per cent for 2025-26, which would be extended to 2027-28.
These budgetary constraints coincide with an unprecedented rise in the number of new practitioners entering the market.
Woo said that previously, only one institution, PolyU, offered a physiotherapy programme, producing 150 bachelor’s degree holders and 48 master’s graduates annually.
But starting in 2020, three other institutions – Hong Kong Metropolitan University, Saint Francis University and Tung Wah College – also launched physiotherapy programmes and, together with PolyU, produced 368 graduates this year.
Each of these three institutions is also set to increase its first-year intake of physiotherapy undergraduates to 175 in September this year.

The return of 200 to 300 foreign-trained physiotherapists to Hong Kong annually also added to the increasing glut of practitioners in a stagnant job market, Woo said.
He cited the example of a remote care facility for elderly residents in Kwu Tung, an area in the North district near the border with Shenzhen, that drew an unprecedented 60 applicants for a single position.
To maintain professional standards amid the oversupply, Woo called on the government to implement a standardised licensing examination for overseas-trained candidates who wanted to practise locally.
Concerns about industry standards spilled onto social media following the release of Joint University Programmes Admissions System (JUPAS) results earlier this month, with prospective students noting that PolyU had accepted candidates with Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) scores below 25 points across their best five subjects.
PolyU’s physiotherapy programme previously required higher scores and Band A placement, with an average intake score of around 30 points in the best five subjects out of a maximum of 35 under a general calculation method where the highest grade amounts to seven points.
Some recent applicants expressed surprise at being admitted despite listing the programme outside their top three preferences.
The lowered threshold caused some students to worry about their future job prospects, as they sensed that the traditionally elite discipline was not only taking in more applicants, but accepting those who chose physiotherapy as a safety option rather than their preferred career.
“I deeply regret choosing physiotherapy four years ago,” one student wrote on Threads. “Now, I may soon become unemployed because the market is saturated … people will pay a price for their choice.”
But Thomson Wong Wai-lung, associate professor and a programme leader at PolyU’s department of rehabilitation sciences, insisted that the university’s standards for accepting physiotherapy undergraduates remained robust.
“This year, about 90 per cent of students were admitted from Band A, with average DSE scores remaining consistently above 30 points for their best five subjects over the years,” he said.
However, according to official statistics, only one student out of 127, or 0.8 per cent of the total, was accepted into the programme last year as a non-Band A admission.

This meant that more than 99 per cent of candidates named the programme as one of their top three choices last year. Wong’s figure of 90 per cent suggested a roughly 9-percentage-point drop in Band A admissions.
But he remained upbeat about graduates’ prospects, saying more than 93 per cent of PolyU’s physiotherapy graduates had been hired in recent years by the Hospital Authority, non-governmental organisations, private clinics and international bodies.
He also emphasised that Hong Kong maintained just 6.4 practising physiotherapists per 10,000 people, lagging far behind comparable economies such as Australia and Japan, which averaged around 16 per 10,000 each.
“This disparity indicates that the underlying demand for rehabilitative services remains strong, offering sustainable, long-term career prospects for well-trained professionals across hospital, community, and private sectors,” he said.

data.title: Ex-care home worker accused of raping intellectually disabled woman 5 times
data.description:
A former assistant warden at a residential home for the intellectually disabled in Hong Kong has been accused of raping a resident multiple times two years ago.
Chung Pui-kei has been charged with five counts of rape of a mentally incapacitated woman who lived at a home in Tai Po linked to the Hong Chi Association, an NGO, between July and August 2024.
Prosecutor Human Lam Hiu-man outlined the five alleged incidents at the High Court on Friday and called a psychiatrist and a clinical psychologist who had examined the woman to testify about her medical history.
A jury of four men and two women has been empanelled, with Judge Douglas Yau Tak-hong presiding over the trial.
Lam said the five incidents had been summarised from two video-recorded police interviews with the woman, known as X, as well as surveillance footage obtained by officers during their investigation.
Lam said X was now 23 years old but had the intellectual ability of a child aged nine years and 10 months.
During the alleged incidents in 2024, X had lived at the residential home, where the defendant worked as an assistant warden.
“From X’s perspective, this child with the intellectual capacity of less than 10 years old would think Kei sir [the defendant] was very friendly with her,” Lam said.
“He would always find her for chats, play video games such as Mario Kart with her and sometimes treat her to marshmallows.”
Three of the alleged rapes took place in a staff room for male employees and two in X’s room, Lam said.
In her opening submission, Lam said the victim had recalled the defendant locking the door, before undressing them both and raping her.
Lam told the court that X remembered feeling pain during some of the rapes and had said no or voiced her discomfort on some occasions. She had not dared to voice out during some instances for fear of being scolded by Chung, Lam said.
The prosecutor said police had found condoms and other items in a locker in the male staff resting room. Officers also identified a bedsheet from a female resident’s room that was found to contain the defendant’s semen and X’s DNA.
Psychiatrist Lydia Lam Yi-ngar of Tai Po Hospital and clinical psychologist Wong Yik-tung of the Social Welfare Department testified about X’s history of mental illness and her condition.
The psychiatrist said she met X twice in 2024 after the alleged incidents, on August 19 and October 21, and prepared a report on her condition for the case.
The doctor said X had been hospitalised in 2018 and 2021 for mental-health issues but had remained stable after taking medication and had required only regular check-ups since her discharge.
Lam also confirmed that she had diagnosed X with bipolar affective disorder.
The psychiatrist told the court that she had assessed X as “not psychotic” at her two check-ups in August and November 2024, and that the mildly intellectually disabled woman did not show any signs of post-traumatic stress disorder.
Defence counsel Lawrence Hui Cheuk-lun asked the psychiatrist whether patients could be prone to hallucinations “affecting the perception of facial features” if they did not take their medication regularly. He also asked whether the doctor knew if X had been taking her medicine regularly in July 2024.
The doctor said hallucinations were not a side effect of valproate sodium, a mood stabiliser that was one of two types of drugs X took, and that although she had relied on information from staff at the residential home on X’s medication, a blood test had shown levels of the drug consistent with the required dosage.
Clinical psychologist Wong, who assessed X’s intellectual capacity after the alleged rapes, will continue giving evidence on Monday.
